title: Kirana and the Mangrove Map
blurb: An old tin box, a hand-drawn map and a rising tide. Kirana follows her grandfather's secret path into the mangrove forest.

chapters.title: The Tin Box
chapters.text:
When the school holidays began, Kirana travelled with her brother Bima to their grandfather's village on the north coast of Java. Opa's house stood on stilts, only a few steps from the sea. At high tide, the water licked the bottom of the wooden ladder.

On the second rainy afternoon, Opa asked the children to tidy the storeroom. Behind a pile of fishing nets, Kirana found a dented biscuit tin. Inside, wrapped in plastic, lay a yellowing sheet of paper.

"It is a map," whispered Bima. The lines were drawn in blue pencil. A wavy coast, little pictures of trees, a tiny boat, and a cross in red ink at the far edge.

Kirana turned the paper over. On the back, in shaky handwriting, someone had written: Follow the tide, not the path.

chapters.title: What Opa Remembered
chapters.text:
At dinner, Kirana placed the map on the table. Opa put on his glasses and said nothing for a long time. Then he smiled, and his eyes shone.

"I drew this when I was twelve," he said. "In those days the sea was angry. The waves had eaten the beach and knocked down half of our houses. The fishermen said the sea took one metre of land every year."

"What is the cross?" asked Bima.

"That is where I planted my first mangrove seedling," said Opa. "An old woman told me that the roots would hold the soil and break the waves. Everybody laughed at me. I planted it anyway."

Kirana's heart began to race. "Is it still there?" she asked.

"I have not been back for years," said Opa. "The path is gone. Only the tide knows the way."

chapters.title: Reading the Tide
chapters.text:
The next morning, Opa showed the children a tide table, which his neighbour had pinned on the wall. It listed the times of high and low water for each day.

"The sea rises and falls twice a day, pulled by the moon," he explained. "At high tide, the mangrove forest is half under water. At low tide, the mud appears, and you can walk between the roots. You must start soon after low tide begins, and you must be out before the water comes back."

Kirana counted on her fingers. "Low tide is at ten o'clock today," she said. "It turns about six hours later."

"Very good," said Opa. "That gives you only a short time. I will lend you my boots. Take a rope, a water bottle and a whistle. And promise me you will turn back at the first sign of the tide."

chapters.title: Into the Roots
chapters.text:
At ten o'clock, the children set off. The sea had gone far away, and the beach was a great grey plain of mud. Bima held the map and Kirana led. Their boots made loud, sucking sounds.

At the edge of the forest, the mangrove roots rose out of the mud like hundreds of arched legs. "They look like spiders," shivered Bima.

"They are called prop roots," said Kirana. "I read about them. They help the tree stand in soft mud and take in air."

Little crabs scuttled away. Small fish with bulging eyes, called mudskippers, jumped across the mud on their fins. Kirana laughed. "They are fish that walk!"

The map said to follow the smallest creek for two hundred steps. They counted aloud together, one, two, three, all the way to the end.

chapters.title: The Wrong Turn
chapters.text:
After two hundred steps, the creek split in two. The map showed only one line, but now there were two. Which one was right?

"We should go left," said Bima. "It looks wider."

Kirana was not sure. She remembered the words on the back. Follow the tide, not the path. She dipped her finger in the water and felt a gentle current in the right-hand creek, flowing towards her and out to sea. The left-hand creek was almost still.

"At low tide, water drains out of the forest," she said. "A creek with a current comes from deep inside, where the water has gathered. Opa drew that one. We go right!"

Bima grumbled, but he followed. After a few minutes, the creek led them to a small clearing. They had arrived! But Kirana's watch said one o'clock. The tide had turned, and brown water had already begun to creep around their boots.

chapters.title: The First Tree
chapters.text:
In the clearing stood a mangrove tree taller than their house. Its trunk was thick and grey, and its branches spread wide. Around it, hundreds of younger trees grew in neat rows. A wooden board, almost covered with moss, read: First tree, planted by Wayan, aged twelve.

"Opa was Wayan!" shouted Bima. "That is his name!"

Kirana touched the rough bark. "He was right," she whispered. "He grew a whole forest."

She blew her whistle three times, as Opa had asked. The sound travelled over the water, and soon the engine of a small boat came closer. Opa had been watching from the sea wall with binoculars. He lifted the children on board.

Opa looked at the tree with wet eyes. "Thank you for finding my little friend," he said. "Now the whole village will know that the laughing was wrong."
